title: The button
tts: Right now, somewhere in the world, millions of people are pressing a button that does absolutely nothing. You have probably pressed one this week. Maybe today. And here's the strange part: it isn't broken. The people who installed it know exactly what it does, and they decided to leave it there anyway. There's one on your street corner. There may be one in your office building. And there's a good chance there's one in the elevator you ride every morning. So why would a city spend money on buttons that do nothing? Who decided this, and why does nobody tell you? By the end of this video, you'll see that a button that does nothing might be one of the cleverest tricks in modern engineering. But first, let's open the case files.

title: Case file one: the crosswalk
tts: Case file number one: the crosswalk button. Traffic engineers have a nickname for it. They call it the beg button, because you're literally asking the light for permission. And for a long time, that button really did work. Back in the middle of the twentieth century, many intersections ran on simple controllers. When you pressed the button, a signal went to a box on the corner, and the light changed sooner, or it gave you a walk sign it wouldn't have given otherwise. Then cities grew. Traffic got heavier. And engineers realized something uncomfortable: if every pedestrian could interrupt the traffic flow at any moment, an entire avenue of carefully timed green lights would fall apart. So, intersection by intersection, the lights were handed over to computers.

title: New York, 2004
tts: And then, in two thousand four, The New York Times did something nobody had done before. It asked the city a simple question: how many of these buttons actually work? The answer was shocking. Out of roughly three thousand two hundred and fifty pedestrian buttons in New York City, more than two thousand five hundred did nothing at all. More than three out of four. Their wires led nowhere useful. The lights around them were timed by a central computer, and no matter how many times you pressed, the walk sign came exactly when the schedule said it would. So why not just take them down? Because removing a single button was estimated to cost several hundred dollars. Multiply that by thousands of corners, and suddenly doing nothing looks like the cheapest plan in the city. So the dead buttons stayed. Many of them are still there.

title: Not all of them
tts: But here's what makes the story more interesting: not every crosswalk button is fake. In quieter neighborhoods and suburbs, the button often really does call the walk sign, because without it, the light would skip the pedestrian phase completely. In some downtowns, the button only works late at night, when the computer switches to a lighter schedule. And many newer buttons have a second job. They click, vibrate or talk, so that blind pedestrians know when it's safe to cross. That means the same yellow box can be a real switch, a part-time switch, an accessibility device, or a decoration, and from the outside, they all look identical. Then, in twenty twenty, the pandemic exposed the secret. Some cities in Australia and the United States set many of their crossings to automatic, so people wouldn't have to touch the buttons at all. And for a lot of pedestrians, nothing changed. The walk sign came on exactly as before.

title: Case file two: the elevator
tts: But the crosswalk isn't the strangest case. Case file number two is inside the building. Step into an elevator, and look at the panel. There's a button with two little arrows pointing at each other: door close. Many of us press it the moment we get in. In a lot of elevators in the United States, during normal operation, that button doesn't make the doors close any faster. One reason is a law. Since nineteen ninety, the Americans with Disabilities Act has required elevator doors to stay open long enough for someone using a cane, a walker or a wheelchair to get in. So the doors run on a timer, and the button can't cut that time short. But the button isn't dead. Insert a special key, and the elevator switches into fire service mode. Now the door close button works perfectly, because in an emergency, firefighters need full control. So the button you press every morning may only truly work for people wearing helmets.

title: Case file three: the thermostat
tts: Case file number three is the one that makes office workers angry. Picture the thermostat on the wall of a big open office. Someone is always too cold, someone is always too hot, and someone is always turning the dial. In two thousand three, The Wall Street Journal reported on a secret that heating and cooling technicians had known for years: some of those office thermostats aren't connected to anything. The temperature of the whole floor is controlled by a central system somewhere else in the building. The box on the wall is there for the people. In a survey by a trade magazine, a large share of technicians admitted they had installed dummy thermostats at least once. And the most surprising detail? After people turned the dial on a fake thermostat, the complaints often went down. Some even said the room felt warmer. The temperature hadn't changed at all. Only the feeling did.

title: The illusion of control
tts: So three different machines, three different industries, and the same strange design choice. Why? To understand it, we need to visit a psychology lab. In the nineteen seventies, the Harvard psychologist Ellen Langer ran a famous experiment with lottery tickets. Some people were simply handed a ticket. Others got to pick their own. Later, when the researchers asked to buy the tickets back, the people who had chosen their ticket demanded several times more money, even though every ticket had exactly the same odds. Langer called this the illusion of control: we feel we can influence things we actually can't, and we value that feeling. Another classic study went even further. People were asked to solve puzzles while being blasted with loud, unpredictable noise. Some of them were given a button that could stop the noise. They performed better and felt less stressed, and here's the twist: most of them never even pressed it. Just knowing they could was enough.

title: Designing the wait
tts: Once you know this, you start seeing it everywhere. Take waiting. Some hotels and office buildings put mirrors next to their elevators, because when people can look at themselves, the wait feels shorter, and complaints drop. One famous story comes from an airport in Houston. Passengers kept complaining that their bags took too long to arrive. The airport added more staff, and the wait went down to about eight minutes, but the complaints didn't stop. Then they tried something else. They moved the arrival gates farther from baggage claim, so passengers had to walk about six times longer. By the time they got there, their bags were almost ready. And the complaints nearly disappeared. The bags didn't come any faster. The waiting just didn't feel like waiting anymore. The same idea lives on your phone. Researchers at Harvard found that people often trust a search more when the website shows it working, with a progress bar and a list of what it's checking, even if the results could appear instantly. They call it the labor illusion.

title: Is it a lie?
tts: So, is a fake button a lie? Critics say yes, and they have a point. If people learn that a button is useless, they may stop trusting every button, including the ones that matter. Some pedestrians who believe the light will never change get impatient and cross on red. Others argue the opposite. A button that does nothing costs almost nothing, it never breaks the traffic plan, and it makes millions of people a little calmer every day. Engineers who design these systems usually don't see it as a trick at all. Their job is to keep traffic moving and people safe, and if a small piece of plastic makes the wait feel shorter, that's a win. And honestly, it's hard to know who's right, because the button works best when you don't know the secret. Which means that by watching this video, you may have just broken a few of them for yourself.

title: So what does it do?
tts: So let's close the case. The crosswalk button in a big city is often connected to nothing but a schedule. The door close button in an elevator may only work for firefighters. The thermostat on the office wall may be talking to no one at all. And yet, every one of them does a job. It turns waiting into doing. It turns helplessness into a small feeling of control. It makes the minute feel shorter and the room feel warmer. So next time you stand at the corner and press that yellow button three times, you'll know the truth. It probably won't change the light. But it was never really built for the light. It was built for you.
